newsitem.title: USA: New Jerusalem housing breeds mistrust - Clinton.
newsitem.headline: New Jerusalem housing breeds mistrust - Clinton.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, starting talks with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, said on Monday he wished Israel had not decided to build new housing for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem because it bred mistrust.

"I would have preferred the decision not have been made because I don't think it builds confidence, I think it builds mistrust," Clinton told reporters at the start of his Oval Office meeting with Arafat.
Clinton gave no indication of what, if anything, he might do to influence the Israelis to change their decision on the matter, which has sparked strong protests by Palestinians.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government decided last week to build 6,500 homes for Jews on Jabal Abu Ghneim, a pine-covered hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem known by Israelis as Har Homa.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East War and views the entire city as its capital, but the Palestinians want East Jerusalem as capital of a future state.

Arafat's visit to the White House was his first since last October, when Clinton met with him and Netanyahu in an effort to revive talks over Israel's much-delayed partial troop withdrawal from the West Bank town of Hebron.
Clinton, noting Israel and the Palestinians eventually came to terms on that troop redeployment, said this was a similarly challenging period for the peace process.

"Because of the efforts that he (Arafat) made in working with the Israelis, an agreement was reached, a timetable was established and we're moving forward," Clinton said. "This is also a difficult moment but I think we can work through it and go forward."

Arafat said on Monday he believed Israel wanted to build the housing to isolate East Jerusalem and appeared to suggest that Israel was seeking to extend its influence toward the town of Bethlehem, now under a form of Palestinian self-rule.
Asked if Israel was seeking with the new housing to make annexation of East Jerusalem a fait accompli, Arafat replied: "Not only for Jerusalem, but also for Bethlehem."
"Because their target is to squeeze and to isolate Jerusalem but (at) the same time to build the settlements (at) the entrance of Bethlehem," Arafat said.
Clinton sought to accent the positive as the meeting with Arafat began, noting the two sides had managed to overcome their differences on Hebron.

In January, Israel and the Palestinians reached an accord on Hebron in which the right-wing Israeli government agreed for the first time to hand over territory Israel occupied in the 1967 Middle East War to PLO rule.

Arafat's meeting with Clinton was part of a group of U.S. visits by Middle East leaders. Netanyahu came to Washington to see Clinton last month, and Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak and Jordan's King Hussein are both scheduled to do so this month.
Arafat left the White House about 90 minutes after he arrived and was scheduled to hold talks at the State Department later on Monday.
